newsitem.title: USA: Scientists seek more cash to track asteroids.
newsitem.headline: Scientists seek more cash to track asteroids.

text.p: The earth could be hit at any time by a deadly asteroid, and governments should urgently fund more programmes to seek them out and find ways of destroying them, British and Australian astronomers said on Tuesday.
Scientists and amateur astronomers met in London to discuss the best ways to track the thousands of asteroids that pass close to the earth every decade.
"People like to imagine that there are battalions of astronomers scouring the skies. There aren't," said Duncan Steel, an astronomer at Australia's University of Adelaide.
Steel said any one person's risk of being killed by such a collision is four times higher than that of being killed in an air crash, although this was due to how statistics work.

The risk is assessed assuming that everyone in the whole world would be killed, which raises the stakes up considerably compared to a plane crash in which only a few hundred die. The risk of an actual asteroid collision is much lower than the risk that a passenger jet will crash.
Nonetheless, some scientists are deeply concerned.
"We really need to get a better idea of what we are doing, what we can do," said Richard Tremaine Smith of the government-funded British National Space Centre.

Steel helped set up the Rome-based Spaceguard Foundation earlier this year to heighten awareness of the asteroid danger. He said it would cost about 20 million pounds ($33 million) to set up a worldwide network of six early warning posts.

"When you sit down and look at the figures you realise it would be crazy not to carry out this programme, because the amount it costs is much, much less than your expectation of loss," he said after the meeting.

Steel complained that a lack of funding could close Australia's programme for scanning the southern hemisphere for the asteroids. A proposed U.S. programme only covers about two percent of the sky, he said.
But just a little bit could greatly increase what was being tracked.

"We need 500,000 pounds ($825,000) to enhance our Schmidt telescope," said Jay Tate, an amateur astronomer and member of the Spaceguard group. "This would mean the discovery of an average of one asteroid each night."
Tate said the United Nations should pay for this, although they have asked the British government for funds.
Then, astronomers could decide if "the big one" was about to destroy the earth. If it was, scientists could send up an atomic bomb to deflect it.
Tate said it would have to be a large bomb. "The ideal time to deflect an asteroid is when it reachest the point nearest the sun in its orbit around the earth," he said.
Tate and Steel say past disasters illustrate the dangers facing the planet.

One is the mysterious 1908 explosion that flattened hundreds of square miles (kilometres) around Tunguska, Siberia. Astronomers think an asteroid or large meteorite exploded on impact with the earth's atmosphere.
Scientists also think a meteor or asteroid impact wiped out the dinosaurs 65 million years ago.
